intro:
This is the audio overview of the Next.js guide. Next.js questions come in two kinds. The first kind is about the model: what runs on the server, what runs in the browser, and what is cached where. The second kind is about versions, because the defaults have changed more than once, and an answer that was right two years ago can be wrong today.

So this overview keeps coming back to one habit. Say which version you mean.

There are nine sections: what changed in version sixteen, App Router fundamentals, rendering strategies, data fetching and caching, routing, server actions, performance, the proxy layer with authentication and deployment, and a deep dive into production concerns.

chapters.title: Next.js 16: What Changed
chapters.text:
Section one is about versions. If you do not remember which version a project uses, say so and check: read the real versions from the package file and the lockfile before the interview. Then know what that version implies.

The headline feature in version sixteen is Cache Components. It is an opt in caching model. With it switched on, a route is rendered at request time by default, and you explicitly mark the parts that can be cached with the use cache directive. Two helpers go with it. Cache life says how long a cached result stays fresh. Cache tag gives it a label, so you can invalidate it later.

Invalidation has three functions, and they differ in how quickly the user sees fresh data and where you may call them. Update tag is for a server action, when the user must see their own change straight away. Revalidate tag marks tagged data as stale so that it is refreshed in the background. Revalidate path does the same for a route.

The request APIs changed as well. Cookies, headers, route parameters and search parameters used to be readable synchronously. Since version fifteen they are promises, because a route can be prerendered before any request exists. Version sixteen removed the temporary synchronous access.

Finally, the request lifecycle. Headers, redirects and rewrites from the configuration file are applied first. Then the proxy file runs. It replaced the middleware file, and it runs on the Node runtime. After that the route is matched and rendered.

chapters.title: App Router Fundamentals
chapters.text:
Section two is App Router fundamentals.

The App Router is built on React Server Components and on a convention of special file names. The page file is the screen for a route. The layout file wraps pages and keeps its state when you navigate between them. The loading file is shown while a page's data is on its way. The error file catches errors in that part of the tree and shows a fallback.

The idea you must be able to explain is the difference between server and client components. Server components are the default. They render entirely on the server, and no JavaScript for them is sent to the browser. They can read a database or a secret directly. They cannot use state, effects or event handlers. Client components are marked with the use client directive at the top of the file. They are rendered on the server for the first response as well, and then made interactive in the browser.

The composition rule is a favourite quiz question. A client component can never import a server component, because everything a client component imports is bundled for the browser. But a server component can be passed to a client component as children, or as another prop. So an interactive wrapper, such as a collapsible panel, can still contain server rendered content.

The practical advice follows from that. Keep the use client boundary as low in the tree as you can. Make the small interactive piece a client component, and leave the page around it on the server.

chapters.title: Rendering Strategies
chapters.text:
Section three covers rendering strategies. They differ in when the page is produced and how fresh the data is.

Static generation produces the page at build time. It is the fastest possible response, served from a content delivery network, and the content is only as fresh as the last build. Server side rendering produces the page on each request. It is always fresh, and every request pays for it. Incremental static regeneration sits between them: serve a cached static result, and regenerate it in the background after a set time, or on demand. Client side rendering sends a shell and fetches data in the browser, which suits private screens behind a login where search engines do not matter.

How you configure regeneration depends on the version, so say which model you mean. In the older model you set a revalidation time on a route or on a fetch. With Cache Components you mark what can be cached and give it a lifetime.

Partial prerendering combines static and dynamic content in one route. The static shell, everything that does not depend on the request, is prerendered and served at once. The dynamic parts stream in afterwards, inside Suspense boundaries.

And know what makes a route dynamic. In the App Router, a route opts into dynamic rendering when it uses request time data such as cookies or headers, or a fetch that asks not to be stored.

In an interview, choose a strategy per route and say why: static for marketing pages, regenerated for a catalogue, per request for a basket.

chapters.title: Data Fetching & Caching
chapters.text:
Section four is data fetching and caching, where most interview answers go wrong.

There are four caching layers. Request memoisation removes duplicate fetches within a single render, so two components asking for the same data cause one request. The data cache stores fetch results on the server across requests. The full route cache stores the rendered output of static routes. And the router cache lives in the browser and keeps visited routes for quick navigation.

The defaults changed between versions. In version fourteen, fetch was cached by default, and people were surprised by stale data after a database change. From version fifteen it is not cached unless you ask. That is why you name your version.

One quiz is worth keeping. To reflect a database change on every page that uses that data, invalidate by tag. Tag based revalidation reaches every cached result with that tag, wherever it is used.

Next, route handlers against server actions. Both run only on the server. A route handler is a real endpoint with an address and methods. You need one for webhooks, and for an API used by anything that is not your own React code. A server action is a function you call from a form or an event handler, meant for changes made from your own interface.

For dynamic routes, one function tells Next.js which parameter values to prerender at build time. A companion setting decides what happens for a value that is not on the list: render it on demand, or return not found.

chapters.title: Routing & Navigation
chapters.text:
Section five is routing and navigation.

Two advanced conventions render more than one thing from a single address. Parallel routes show several independent pages in the same layout at once, such as a dashboard with separate panels that load and fail independently. Intercepting routes show a route inside the current layout. The usual example is a photo that opens in a modal over the feed when you click it, and opens as a full page when you load its address directly.

The link component prefetches. When a link scrolls into view, Next.js fetches the code for that route, and for static routes its data too, so navigation feels instant. The push function on the router is for navigating from code, for example after a form succeeds. It does not prefetch by itself.

Three hooks read routing state, and all three work only in client components. The router hook gives you navigation from code: push, replace, refresh and back. The pathname hook gives you the current path, which is how you highlight the active link. The search parameters hook reads the query string.

Metadata, meaning the title, the description, the social preview tags and the canonical address, is defined in server components and not by writing a head element by hand. Export a fixed object when the values are known. Export an async function when they depend on data, such as a product name. Next.js removes the duplicate work, so fetching the same product for the metadata and for the page costs one request.

chapters.title: Server Actions & Mutations
chapters.text:
Section six is server actions and mutations.

A server action is a function marked to run on the server, which you can use as the action of a form or call from an event handler. Its lifecycle is worth being able to narrate. The form submits, or the call starts inside a transition. That triggers a post request to the current page address, carrying an encrypted id for the action and its arguments. The server runs the function: it authenticates, authorises, validates, changes the data and invalidates what is now stale. The response carries the updated interface, and React applies it without a full page reload.

Two hooks make the form pleasant. The form status hook tells a component whether the form it sits in is being submitted, which is how a submit button disables itself. It must be called in a component nested inside the form. The action state hook holds what the action returned, such as validation messages, so you can show them next to the fields.

Now the point that interviewers probe hardest. A server action compiles to a public endpoint. Anyone can call it directly with a crafted request, without ever seeing your interface. Hiding the delete button from people who are not the author protects nothing. So every action must validate its input again and check authorisation again, on the server, every time.

Say that sentence in any security discussion about Next.js. It shows you understand that the directive marks where code runs, and is not a security boundary.

chapters.title: Performance & Optimization
chapters.text:
Section seven is performance and optimisation, three tools that each fix a specific problem.

The image component handles what a plain image element leaves to you. It produces responsive sizes, so a phone does not download a desktop image. It loads images lazily when they are below the visible part of the page. It converts to modern formats on demand. And it prevents layout shift by requiring a width and height, so the browser reserves the space before the image arrives. For the main image at the top of a page, tell it to load with priority, because lazy loading that one hurts your largest paint.

Streaming with Suspense improves how fast a page feels. Without streaming, the whole page waits for its slowest piece of data before any of it is sent. With Suspense boundaries around the slow parts, Next.js sends the fast shell at once, with fallbacks in the gaps, and streams each slow part in when it is ready. The total time may be the same. The user sees something useful much sooner.

The font module downloads font files at build time and serves them from your own site. That removes the extra round trip to a third party font server on every visit, and it is better for privacy, because no request goes to that third party. It also sets up a fallback font with matching measurements, which reduces the jump when the real font loads.

In an interview, connect each tool to a metric: images to the largest paint, fonts and reserved sizes to layout shift, and streaming to how soon the first content appears.

chapters.title: Proxy (Middleware), Auth & Deployment
chapters.text:
Section eight is short: the proxy layer, runtimes and where code runs.

Middleware is code that runs before a request completes, before a page or a route handler renders. It is the place for redirects when someone is not signed in, for assigning a cookie for an experiment, for rewrites based on language or location, and for changing headers. Version sixteen renamed it. The file is now called proxy, and it runs on the Node runtime.

Its constraints matter more than its features. It runs on every matching request, so it must be cheap. Do a quick check on a cookie there. Do not query a database there. And do not treat it as your only authorisation check. It is a first filter. The real check belongs next to the data.

Then the two runtimes. The Node runtime is the default. You get the full Node API, any package, database drivers and native modules. The Edge runtime runs in lightweight isolates that start very quickly, close to the user, with a smaller, web standard set of APIs. Many packages do not run there, and neither do most database drivers.

How do you choose? Use Node unless you have a reason not to. Choose Edge for small, fast logic that benefits from running near the user and needs nothing beyond the web standard APIs. If a route talks to a database in one region, running the code at the edge can make it slower, because every query then has to travel back to that region.

chapters.title: Deep Dive: Production Next.js
chapters.text:
The deep dive covers what you meet in production.

Authentication and authorisation. Next.js recommends a data access layer: one server only module that verifies the session and performs every read and write together with an authorisation check. Pages, server actions and route handlers all go through it, so no path to the data skips the check.

Error handling. Expected errors, such as failed validation or an email already taken, should be returned from a server action and shown in the form. They should not be thrown. Unexpected errors are thrown and caught by the nearest error file. A global error file covers the root layout, and a not found file handles missing content.

Route handlers run per request by default. A handler for the get method can opt into static caching, and other methods are never cached. They can also stream a response, and they are where webhooks arrive.

Environment variables are server only by default. A database address is available in server code and is never sent to the browser. Variables with the public prefix are placed into the browser bundle at build time, so never put a secret behind that prefix.

The after function schedules work to run once the response has been sent, so logging and analytics do not delay the user.

Last, hosting it yourself. The standalone output option produces a minimal server with only the dependencies it needs. You copy the public folder and the static assets beside it, or serve them from a content delivery network. With several instances, remember that they must share one cache, or each will serve its own version of the truth.
